label: systems thinking and process improvement
overview: Systems and process improvement scenarios typically present as one of three underlying problems: the client is applying symptomatic fixes to recurring issues without addressing the structural root cause; they are scaling operations without first stabilising the systems that underpin them; or they are misreading feedback data and overreacting in ways that introduce new instability. The foundational principle across all systems work is that businesses are Complex Adaptive Systems — not linear machines — and that structure influences behaviour. Fixing the structure fixes the behaviour. The golden rule is Systems Before Scale. This domain holds four materials: the underlying causal theory, the choice of systems philosophy, the six-system map used to locate the problem, and the five-step method for redesigning a process.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the problem that the client keeps fixing the same issue repeatedly, that they are trying to scale before their systems are stable, or that process changes are creating unexpected downstream consequences?
diagnostic_entry.recurring_symptomatic_fixes: If the client is patching the same problem repeatedly — discounting to manage complaints, rehiring for roles that keep failing — the issue is a structural loop, not a personnel or pricing problem. Introduce Circles of Causality and the Shifting the Burden archetype before recommending any process change.
diagnostic_entry.scaling_before_systems_are_ready: If the client wants to grow but their current processes are inconsistent or volatile — apply the Systems Before Scale principle. Use the 5-step framework to stabilise first. A business cannot safely scale if it has not resolved its underlying volatility.
diagnostic_entry.process_changes_creating_new_problems: If a recent process change has caused unexpected ripple effects — over-hiring after a demand surge, or instability weeks after a rollout — the client is experiencing feedback loop delays. Use the delay concept from Circles of Causality to reframe the problem before recommending further changes.

materials.name: Systems Thinking and Circles of Causality
materials.summary: Moves the client from linear problem-solving to circular thinking, so they can see how the structure of their own business keeps producing the problem they are trying to fix. Built on Peter Senge's Circles of Causality: A affects B, which feeds back to affect A, so the effect becomes the cause. The governing principle is that structure influences behaviour — different people in the same broken structure produce the same broken results.
materials.who_when: Use before recommending any process redesign — with clients who keep hitting the same problem, whose last process change produced unexpected consequences, or who are blaming staff for an outcome the structure is generating.
steps: Reframe from linear to circular — instead of asking what caused this, map how A affects B and how B feeds back to A.
Separate process from system: a process produces one component consistently (a car's engine), a system is interdependent processes acting as a whole (the finished car).
Treat the business as a Complex Adaptive System, not a machine — its parts adapt, so collaborative principles work where static step-by-step models fail.
Name the loop — Reinforcing (amplifies change into growth or a death spiral, like a platform whose users make it more valuable) or Balancing (seeks equilibrium and resists change, like a thermostat).
Look for the delay — the lag between action and feedback that makes leaders oversteer, such as hiring hard through a temporary surge and carrying the overhead afterwards.

Test against the two archetypes — Limits to Growth (a reinforcing loop meets a constraint and plateaus) and Shifting the Burden (a symptomatic fix removes the pressure to fix the structure, so the problem returns).
Map it as a Causal Loop Diagram so the team can see how the parts interact, and find the leverage points where a small change produces lasting improvement.
Name the negative forces the plan will generate even if executed perfectly, and make measuring them part of the KPIs so the client gets a balanced report.
Standardise how the feedback data is read — following Deming on volatility, plan for predictable events in advance and do not over-react to the numbers.

materials.name: Three Systems Philosophies
materials.summary: Selects the philosophy that should govern the client's process design, so the operating model matches what the business actually promises its customers. The choice follows the market promise, not preference or industry convention: Six Sigma removes variation, Lean thinking removes frills, and the Theory of Constraints exploits the system's weakest point.
materials.who_when: Clients designing or redesigning their operating model — best settled before any flowcharting begins.
steps: Establish the client's market and customer promise in their own words before proposing any philosophy.
If the promise is mass-market consistency with no surprises, choose Six Sigma and design to remove variation — McDonald's, where every burger is the same everywhere.
If the promise is to save the customer money by removing frills, choose Lean thinking and strip out everything that does not add value — Pak n Save.

If the strategy is to combine niches into a unique experience, choose the Theory of Constraints and design to exploit the system's weaknesses — Airbnb, combining unused private property with traveller demand.
Carry the chosen philosophy into the process design so the architecture and the customer promise stay consistent with each other.

materials.name: Six Business Systems
materials.summary: A map of the six interdependent systems every business runs on — Planning, Data, Marketing, Sales, People and Process — used to locate which one is actually generating the client's problem before any specific process work begins. The rule governing all six is Systems Before Scale: growth applied to a broken system amplifies the breakage.
materials.who_when: Any client presenting an operational, efficiency or process problem, and any client considering growth — use it as the entry framework before narrowing to one process.
steps: Walk the client through all six systems so the conversation covers the whole business rather than the loudest symptom — Planning (direction), Data (measurement), Marketing (acquisition), Sales (revenue capture), People (capability), Process (delivery).
Locate which of the six is the actual source of the problem, rather than the one where the pain is being felt.
Assess the stability of that system and the ones it depends on — the six are interdependent and rarely fail in isolation.
Apply Systems Before Scale — if the client is planning growth, confirm the underlying systems are stable before endorsing any expansion.
Prioritise the system to work on first, then move to the five-step framework for the specific process inside it.

materials.name: 5-Step Process Implementation Framework
materials.summary: The method for designing, testing and rolling out a new or improved process. The two things that matter most in any system are its design and its feedback loop, and the most common failure is skipping the pilot. Because a business is a human system, the change is embedded by coaching the team through it — not by issuing a document.
materials.who_when: Clients ready to redesign a specific process, once the philosophy is chosen and the target system identified — work all five steps in sequence.
steps: Identify the focus area — pick processes that truly matter: health and safety exposure, strict compliance, or where a major performance jump is needed. Assess cause and effect, observe bottlenecks, and isolate the components before designing anything.
Design the architecture — break the process into Nodes (action steps) and Links (sequence or decision branches), and hold it to 5–13 Nodes: fewer lacks detail, more overloads the team.

Test the layout physically — write the dominant Nodes on sticky notes and shift them around to check the logical order really is the smartest one, add visual references, and write measurable objectives before finalising.

Pilot before rollout — never replace an old system company-wide at once. Run a controlled test with a small group, coach in chunks by demonstrating the behaviour, and measure against the metrics set beforehand.
Roll out in progressive stages — quantify the behavioural change sought and win genuine buy-in from the people who will use it; discipline and regular training are what make results consistent.

Review and refine — close the feedback loop through observation, financial metrics and KPIs, fold in the feedback of the people working the process, and plan for predictable volatility so nobody overreacts to normal variation.
For high-risk processes, build in redundant systems so a whole section can shut down safely or be swapped for an alternate in a major failure, rather than taking the business down with it.

advisor_guidance.systems_before_scale: The single most common error in growth conversations is recommending expansion before the client's existing systems are stable. Scaling a broken system amplifies the breakage. Always audit the six business systems for stability before endorsing growth plans.
advisor_guidance.blame_the_structure_not_the_person: When a client is frustrated with a team member or a supplier, investigate whether the system structure is generating the poor result before attributing it to individual failure. Different people placed in the same broken structure produce the same broken results — the fix is structural, not personnel.
advisor_guidance.symptomatic_fixes_compound: Every time a client applies a symptomatic fix — discounting to stop a complaint, manually correcting a recurring data error — they remove the pressure that would otherwise force the system to evolve. The problem will return because the underlying loop has not changed. Name the archetype: Shifting the Burden.
advisor_guidance.delays_cause_overreaction: Process changes often appear not to be working because the feedback loop contains a delay. The client over-corrects before the system has had time to respond. When a client reports that a new process made things worse, check whether they are reacting to a delay rather than a genuine failure of the design.
advisor_guidance.coaching_over_documentation: A written process manual alone will not embed new behaviour. The team must be coached through the change — demonstrated, chunked, observed, and given immediate feedback. Buy-in is not created by presenting information; it is created by involving the team in building and refining the process.
